extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literature, philosophy, and creative writers interested in aesthetic and moral criteria for poetry and fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging poetry, drama, and imaginative prose, drawn from a critical discussion of Plato’s objections and counterarguments about the nature, moral effect, and social role of art. Useful for writers and critics considering artistic truth, moral purpose, verisimilitude, and form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation and distance from truth
rubrics_metrics.description: “The poet or painter is an imitator, and in the third degree removed from the truth.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato's objection: imitative art presents appearances, not tested by rule and measure. Modern counter: art may not be mere imitation but an expression of the ideal in sensible forms; an artist can ennoble ordinary subjects (examples: Rembrandt, Turner). Discussion includes whether sculptural exemplars (Pheidias) transcend mere imitation by embodying higher proportion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotive versus rational content
rubrics_metrics.description: “Imitative arts ... express the emotional rather than the rational part of human nature.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato objects that arts stimulate passions and offer opportunity for indulgence rather than rational improvement. The text contrasts this with Aristotle’s catharsis (purgation by pity and fear) and argues that expression can sometimes cure or strengthen emotions; thus the emotional emphasis is ambivalent and must be judged by its effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artist's power to ennoble the commonplace
rubrics_metrics.description: “The artist may ennoble the bed which he paints by the folds of the drapery, or by the feeling of home which he introduces.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A criterion of artistic value: the capacity to impart dignity, pathos or ideal interest to ordinary or humble subjects. Examples cited: Rembrandt giving dignity to a ruined mill or straw-built shed; Turner imparting poignancy to a ship's hull.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embodiment of ideal form and proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: Great works of art seem to be the visible embodiment of the divine; their rule of proportion is ‘higher far than any geometry or arithmetic could express.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art may aim at expressing an ideal order or proportion that transcends literal geometry; such embodiment gives works enduring significance (example: Zeus or Athene of Pheidias). This is a test of greatness beyond mere likeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic power vs moral/mental firmness
rubrics_metrics.description: “Great dramatic or even great rhetorical power is hardly consistent with firmness or strength of mind; dramatic talent is often incidentally associated with a weak or dissolute character.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato’s suspicion that dramatic excellence may correlate with moral weakness (and his disparaging view of actors as losing their own character) poses a criterion: evaluate whether artistic brilliance undermines or reflects the artist's ethical seriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particulars versus universals (authority to teach life)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets are concerned with particulars of sense and are on a level with their own age; they cannot be made a rule of life by legitimate interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato denies poets the authority to prescribe conduct because they deal with particulars, not universals; the text contrasts this with Aristotle’s claim that poetry (concerned with universals) can be truer than history. Use this to judge whether a work aspires to universal truth or merely mirrors its time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political/moral allegiance and susceptibility to patronage
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets are representatives of falsehood, ‘friends of the tyrant,’ and often bask in the sunshine of patronage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess literature for whether it propagates corrupting or sycophantic ideas, panders to rulers, or functions as propaganda. Historical context: poets at court can be complicit with despotism; critics should note whether art resists or abets power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art as compromise between representation and ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: “All imitative art is subject to certain limitations, and therefore necessarily partakes of the nature of a compromise. Something of ideal truth is sacrificed for the sake of the representation, and something in the exactness of the representation is sacrificed to the ideal.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how a work balances fidelity to particulars against aspiration to an ideal: neither perfect realism nor pure abstraction is attainable, and the tension is a structural feature to be judged for success or failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enlisting feeling on the side of reason
rubrics_metrics.description: The vocation of art is to present thought in the form of feeling, to enlist the feelings on the side of reason, to inspire courage or resignation, and perhaps to suggest a sense of infinity and eternity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A positive criterion: art that makes feeling serve thought and moral or intellectual ends—evoking feelings that educate or elevate rather than merely gratify—counts as higher art. Beware of works that merely indulge base appetites under aesthetic guise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Therapeutic/cathartic value of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: “We may sometimes cure disordered emotions by giving expression to them; and that they often gain strength when pent up within our own breast.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether expression in a work functions to alleviate or intensify passions; consider whether depiction of emotion is constructive (healing, clarifying) or merely provocative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enduring or permanent element
rubrics_metrics.description: “Works of art have a permanent element; they idealize and detain the passing thought, and are the intermediates between sense and ideas.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge works by whether they capture and preserve essential truths or feelings beyond their immediate context—whether they have an element that endures and mediates between transient perception and lasting insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical situatedness and changing function
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry ‘holds a different place at different periods of the world’s history’—in infancy it is the whole of literature, in modern times it is often the shadow or echo of its former self.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a work in light of its historical moment and the evolving role of genres; a form once central may now function differently (e.g., poetic features migrating to prose/rhetoric).

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and risk of theme exhaustion
rubrics_metrics.description: Concern whether recurring dominant themes (e.g., the tale of love) may be exhausted after many variations and lose interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether a writer renews exhausted themes by new insight or technique, or merely repeats clichéd variations; freshness of treatment is a criterion of continuing value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness to religious and philosophical truth
rubrics_metrics.description: “Art cannot claim to be on a level with philosophy or religion, and may often corrupt them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether artistic representation distorts, trivializes, or supports central religious/philosophical truths. Some movements/religions renounce images because formal representations can mislead; consider whether form suits subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's highest practical aims
rubrics_metrics.description: A poetry which would be ‘the hymn of divine perfection’—renew youth, find materials in the living present and the past, subdue intractable materials of modern civilisation, elicit simple principles (essential forms) of truth and justice, preserve the good and leave the bad unsung, and be based on a clear insight into the nature of man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This cluster of aspirational criteria sets a high standard: poetry should uplift and educate, integrate present and past, produce moral clarity, celebrate virtues while ignoring harmful excesses, and rest on psychological and ethical insight. Examples: Aeschylus, Sophocles, Milton, Wordsworth, Hebrew prophets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union of feeling (love) with intellectual/ethical purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The tale of love might be ‘two in one, united in the pursuit of knowledge, or the service of God and man; and feelings of love might still be the incentive to great thoughts and heroic deeds.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether affective material (love, passion) is integrated with higher aims—knowledge, service, heroism—rather than mere sentimentality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic freedom versus moralizing
rubrics_metrics.description: “Moralizing in verse is not poetry.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the poet's legitimate creative freedom and resistance to didactic clumsiness, while still asking whether the poet’s freedom is ethically responsible—how can the poetic gift be devoted to the good of mankind without degenerating into mere sermonizing?

rubrics_metrics.name: Verisimilitude and ‘touches of nature’
rubrics_metrics.description: Small verisimilar details—coincidences, precise timings, passing remarks, human foibles—‘add greatly to the probability of the narrative’ and win credibility for marvels and apparitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete, plausible touches (a Defoe technique) to lend credibility to extraordinary events; internal consistency and lifelike detail increase reader belief and emotional engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and consistency in symbolic or mythic cosmology
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions that mix modes (astronomy mingled with symbolism and mythology) risk inconsistency; an orrery/picture of the heavens that is both picture and machine can be ‘necessarily inconsistent with itself.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating mythic or symbolic systems (cosmologies, allegories), ensure internal coherence or acknowledge the tensions deliberately; unclear or contradictory cosmography undermines plausibility and reader comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of choice, wisdom, and moral agency
rubrics_metrics.description: The order of lots indicates chance, but ‘chance may be overcome by the wisdom of man’; virtue founded on habit is insufficient—‘he must add to virtue knowledge’—and freedom of the will within necessity is affirmed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character construction should allow for responsible choice and the development of wisdom; depict how habit, knowledge, and deliberation interact, and avoid reducing moral action to mere routine or fate.
